description: A two-panel hand-drawn schematic (3D block diagram) illustrating martensitic transformation during tensile deformation of an experimental low-density steel; both panels are conceptual diagrams with no axes, scale bars or numeric values. Each panel shows the same rectangular 3D polycrystalline block, with black arrows at the top and bottom pointing vertically outward to indicate the tensile loading direction. (a) Before deformation: the block is a polygonal grain network in which gray grains are labelled "F" (ferrite matrix), two central blocky white grains are labelled "A" (austenite), and three elongated red grains adjacent to them are also labelled "A" (lath-like austenite). (b) The same block after deformation: the two white blocky "A" grains now carry closely spaced parallel line hatching and are relabelled "M" in blue/cyan, i.e. transformed to martensite, while the red lath-like grains remain untransformed and still labelled "A"; no other microstructural change is drawn. The figure therefore demonstrates that under tensile strain the blocky austenite at the ferrite triple edges transforms to martensite first, whereas the lath-like austenite does not transform, matching the caption's colour key (martensite blue, ferrite gray, blocky austenite white, lath-like austenite red).

observations.observation: Both panels are 3D block schematics of the same polycrystalline volume, with vertical black arrows at the top and bottom faces indicating the tensile loading axis.
In (a) the block contains gray grains labelled 'F', two white blocky grains labelled 'A' in the centre, and red elongated grains labelled 'A' near the white grains.
In (b) the previously white blocky 'A' grains are redrawn with dense parallel line hatching and labelled 'M' in blue/cyan, indicating transformation to martensite.
The red lath-like grains remain unchanged and still labelled 'A' in both (a) and (b), so they are drawn as untransformed after deformation.
Neither panel contains axes, scale bars, numeric data labels or legends; the only text is the grain labels A, F and M.
The caption states the colour key: martensite marked in blue, ferrite delineated in gray, blocky austenite in white and lath-like austenite in red.
The caption states (a) is the state before deformation and (b) corresponds to deformation inducing austenite rotation and transformation (A austenite, F ferrite, M martensite).

The citing text reports that blocky austenite grains had a high Schmid factor and were positioned at the ferrite triple edges, whereas lath-like austenite lay between ferrite laths or was embedded inside a single ferrite grain with a lower Schmid factor.

The citing text states that with increasing tensile strain the blocky austenite transformed first into martensite because of higher localized stress, favoured by the triaxial stress state at ferrite triple junction boundaries.

The citing text states that lath-like austenite with a lower Schmid factor rotated firstly during deformation, depending on the crystallographic orientation of the grains with respect to the straining direction; the schematic itself shows these grains as still austenite in (b).

The figure supports the argument that the two austenite morphologies behave differently under tension: blocky austenite (white, panel (a)) transforms to martensite (blue-hatched 'M', panel (b)) while lath-like austenite (red) persists as austenite.

subfigures.description: Undeformed 3D block schematic: gray polygonal grains labelled 'F' (ferrite), two blocky white grains labelled 'A' (austenite) in the centre, and three elongated red grains also labelled 'A' (lath-like austenite) adjacent to them. Vertical outward-pointing black arrows at top and bottom mark the tensile loading direction.

Same 3D block after deformation: the two white blocky grains now contain dense parallel line hatching and are labelled 'M' in blue/cyan (martensite), while the red lath-like grains remain labelled 'A' and unhatched. Grey ferrite grains and the loading arrows are unchanged.
